In recent years, advanced time series models have gained popularity for predicting electricity consumption. We investigate the applicability of ARIMA and LSTM models in forecasting hourly electricity usage during a period of power crisis in Poland. Notably, our analysis reveals that both models are capable of predicting, but their effectiveness is influenced by the length of the forecasting horizon. We found that ARIMA models perform better for shorter-term forecasts, while LSTM models are more accurate for longer-term predictions. However, LSTM models benefit from prior knowledge of future values, which is not the case when they are used without this information. We suggest that combining ARIMA and LSTM models could offer improved predictions. Additionally, our exploration into what makes up an optimal training set for LSTM model learning revealed that a training set comprising data from the last two years of a dataset is particularly effective. We discovered that using the average values of past data is a better approach than using past data itself when it comes to training LSTM models. Furthermore, our comparison of regression analysis and LSTM models identified the latter as the better choice for forecasting, despite the positive results achieved through a combination of ARIMA and LSTM models. We were also unable to demonstrate the statistical significance of an LSTM model's predictions but found that its confidence intervals are not applicable in this context. We propose three potential directions for future research: selecting the optimal sub-datasets for training LSTM models, utilizing a hybrid approach that pairs time series and machine learning techniques, and exploring the theoretical underpinnings of the power crisis phenomenon. Graph-based representations have been widely adopted in program analysis due to their versatility in representing complex graph structures as nodes and edges with arbitrary relationships. Despite this feasibility, implementing a deep learning architecture that effectively captures program information from flow diagrams is a challenging task. Current approaches relying on attention mechanisms, recurrent networks, and spatial temporal convolution have shown some success, but their limitations have hindered further exploration. In an effort to address these constraints, we introduce a novel convolutional neural network, GRCNN, designed to generate code from flow diagrams by recognizing program graphs. By combining graph attention, self-attention, and spatial temporal convolutional layers with spatial auto-readers, GRCNN is well-equipped to capture triangular structural signal patterns, ultimately demonstrating superior performance in deep learning-based method development. Experimental evaluations of our approach, compared to previous methods, reveal a significant increase in accuracy and time efficiency, with an average gain of 6.3% and 4.2 times respectively, without compromising the program analysis's fidelity. Furthermore, analyses using widely adopted evaluation metrics confirm our approach's superior performance, emphasizing the role of graph recognition in deep learning-based methods. Our proposed architecture, accompanied by an open-source implementation, shows great potential in deep learning-based program analysis and other graph recognition tasks. Moreover, this research is expected to pave the way for further techniques in this domain. With ongoing advancements in this area, we envision a future where graph recognition deep learning models like GRCNN are widely integrated into programming tools, ultimately contributing to improved software development efficiency. The digestive system's intricate network poses significant challenges to researchers, from accurately mapping its internal structure to predicting the progression of diseases. Advances in medical imaging technology, particularly the widespread adoption of CT scans, have facilitated rapid and non-invasive examination of the gastrointestinal tract. However, manually tracing the digestive organs in CT images is a labor-intensive process. Researchers have begun to explore the potential of artificial intelligence for automating digestive system segmentation. This study delves into the latest developments in this field, presenting successful applications of deep learning techniques on the digestive system and identifying areas for further research. Our in-house database contains CT scans of patients with various abdominal pathologies, enabling us to demonstrate a deep learning approach for segmenting the gastrointestinal tract. Our results indicate that a convolutional neural network trained on our dataset achieved a dice similarity coefficient of 0.842 for the liver, 0.881 for the spleen, 0.874 for the kidneys, and 0.588 for the gastrointestinal tract. Our findings suggest that deep learning can significantly streamline clinical applications, ultimately improving the accuracy of clinical diagnoses and treatments. This study laid the groundwork for future research on the application of deep learning to the digestive system using diverse medical imaging modalities. We intend to make our database available to the medical community, and our segmentation approach will be made publicly available on a designated platform. Compositional data sets consist of multiple parts that depend on each other, such as percentages or ratios, and must be analyzed together. This work focuses on linear combinations of compositional data variables, taking into account their inherent relationships. It's essential to understand how variables within a data set behave when they are inherently interconnected. This study explores linear combinations of compositional data variables through a mathematical and statistical analysis, highlighting the significance of interpreting results with the constraints imposed by these relationships. A proposed method for communicating these relationships, using Galerkin vectors, is presented, and its application demonstrated using the UCI repository's data on Mexican ground motion. This has been implemented in an R package called compBayes. Experimental findings suggest that considering the inherent relationships among variables yields lower variability and better performance than other combination methods, and the proposed approach offers a valuable tool for data examination, fitting, and interpretation. The underlying mathematical concepts, such as linear independence and dependency, dependent eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and Galerkin vectors, are introduced and explained. The method's interpretation is not confined to compositional data but also applies to other multi-variable data sets with inherent relationships. The proposed technique, named CompBayes, is now available as an R package. The source code is available at https://github.com/krishnacomp/compBayes. The findings of this study have far-reaching implications for developing effective learning systems that mimic biological intelligence. We re-evaluate the process of global aggregation in machine learning through the lens of optimal transport, considering an idealized scenario with a finite number of data points. A key challenge arises from the issue of existence, stemming from the infinite-dimensional nature of the problem. To address this, we draw parallels with the concept of minimal transports in R^n. However, our analysis reveals that these two scenarios exhibit distinct properties: the first is resolved through the principle of optimality, whereas the second poses an existence question. In the optimal transport community, this issue is addressed by introducing the concept of cyclic minimality. In this work, we adapt this concept to our context, demonstrating that minimal transports indeed exist and are unique, and we also establish a closure property. Furthermore, we identify a set of conditions that guarantee the uniqueness of global aggregates. We then apply these findings to the analysis of several global aggregation methods, providing a fresh perspective on the topic. In particular, we reanalyze the generalized mean and the bi-gamma mean under our new framework, and we also introduce a novel global aggregation method, inspired by a quadratic potential function, that we refer to as the Q-gamma mean. We evaluate the performance of these methods on several real-world datasets, showcasing their advantages and limitations. The integration of optimal transport tools into the analysis of global aggregation algorithms sheds new light on their behavior and may guide their future development. The presented results are part of the authors' ongoing research and have not been previously published. The source code to replicate the experiments is available at https://github.com/juliusfischer/plottable. An early version of this work has been made available on arXiv for feedback from the community. The optimized version will be submitted for publication in International Journal of Computer Vision. The authors welcome comments and corrections. The optimal transport community is encouraged to explore the interconnectedness of this work and share their insights. In particular, we draw the attention of the machine learning community to the authors' contribution to the analysis of global aggregation, while inversely drawing the attention of the optimal transport community to the practical implications of this work. The analysis is self-contained, and readers from either community may safely skip the parts that are specific to their own field. The authors believe that this exchange of knowledge has the potential to yield new and interesting perspectives. Pre-training is typically done using a vast image dataset, either for object classification or depth assessment in a monocular setting. We investigated whether training on monocular depth cues alone could better prepare models for semantic segmentation than classification pre-training. To answer this question, we developed a new dataset called NewDepth, consisting of 37,000 high-quality images along with their depth maps, and compared the effectiveness of pre-training methods on the SUN397 and NewDepth datasets using multiple metrics. Our analysis revealed that training on monocular depth cues, particularly those combined with motion fields, consistently provided a stronger pre-training effect than classification, ultimately yielding a 4.5% and 3.6% improvement in segmentation performance on benchmark datasets, respectively. To further validate the potential of pre-training on depth cues, we translated the depth maps in NewDepth and benchmark datasets into pixel values, achieving a remarkable 72.5% mIoU on the SUN397 dataset. The ability to generate compelling stories from numerical data such as stock prices or weather forecasts has fascinating potential. While there has been a recent surge in neural-based approaches to time-series storytelling, many existing methods are limited by their reliance on domain-specific story templates and linear narrative structures. To address this, we introduce TCube, a novel neural framework that can automatically identify and arrange key events in a story using a shared, universal set of concepts. TCube achieves this by training a semantic memory module that captures common patterns across various time-series datasets. Through human evaluation, TCube has outperformed existing methods by 44.4% in creating engaging stories with clear structures and demonstrating strong generalization capabilities across different data streams. To further demonstrate TCube's capabilities, we also developed 14 stories together using numerical data related to the population counts of New York City over a period of 15 years. This research presents a novel model for Japanese term segmentation that employs a longer-term memory buffer to store temporary segmentations. The proposed NMT-based approach significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy, while its memory efficiency is improved by leveraging character-level representations. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this model excels in a setting with available word-level labels and also when training with character-level supervision alone. Furthermore, the proposed model showcases a significant performance boost when compared to previous methods designed specifically for Japanese term segmentation. Importantly, this model's success is achieved without any tailored components, thereby confirming the importance of the concept of short-term memory in Japanese term segmentation. Additionally, the paper includes a blurb on the potential link between the proposed model and human cognitive abilities. The model has been put to use in a Japanese language model that is currently offered through the API services of AI Shack Inc. under the name 'JA-Shiny'. This model has been used in various commercial applications since July 2021.

Medical sign extraction holds significant importance in understanding clinical cases and developing treatment strategies, yet its application is limited due to differences in data presentation across institutions. Signs can be described using varied terms within different domains, making it a challenging task to extrapolate insights from one domain to another. To overcome this issue, domain generalization can be employed, and our approach excels in this realm by adapting to unseen domains through the intentional concealment of features. By collecting unlabelled data from multiple domains and establishing a generalizable model that performs well across these domains without requiring explicit category information, our method surpasses those of the state-of-the-art in sign event extraction while also yielding improved efficiency. Our evaluations demonstrate enhanced performance on various datasets, and a further study reveals our approach to be more effective in dealing with unseen domains compared to conventional techniques. To ensure the trustworthiness of our method, we also introduce a set of automatic tests. As the demand for automated transportation continues to grow, researchers are delving into the challenges of developing an autonomous vehicle navigation system that can adapt to various situations on the road. To address this issue, a significant advancement would be to create a computer program that can navigate through unseen environments after being trained with a Profound Reinforcement Learning system. This innovative approach utilizes an autoencoder-based neural network to compress the vehicle's sensory data, effectively simplifying the input and thus reducing the complexity of the navigation problem. This study evaluates the effectiveness of this Profound Reinforcement Learning system by simulating an autonomous vehicle's training in a 2D navigation task. The results demonstrate that our proposed system achieves a notable 90% success rate in navigating a new, unseen environment following training. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with a similar reinforcement learning method reveals that our approach accelerates training, resulting in a more efficient navigation system. This study examines the ability of linear classifiers to effectively capture the intricate patterns within the item space for the task of cold start in recommendation systems. It involves analyzing data generated by the Shapley transformation, a method that produces highly nonlinear structures. Our findings indicate that linear classifiers can successfully model these complex patterns, and their performance can be optimized by applying a straightforward technique. We also present a simple approach for determining the optimal degree of the item space shapes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed linear classifier, as well as its comparable runtime and data requirements, relative to non-linear models. Notably, linear classification offers significant advantages in both its interpretability and computational efficiency. We support our empirical observations with theoretical justifications that quantify the dependence of linear classification performance on the degree of the item space shape. This theoretical analysis also reveals how the Shapley transformation generates highly nonlinear structures and explains why item similarity tends to be negative. We conduct additional experiments to evaluate the performance of linear classification in real-world recommendation systems and find similar outcomes. Overall, our results illustrate the capability of linear classifiers to effectively model complex patterns within item space and their potential to replace non-linear models, provided that the item space shapes capture the intricacies of the data, without incurring the higher computational costs associated with non-linear models. The code for our work is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/Linear-Item-Space-Shapes. For an earlier version of this study, please see our arXiv submission: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10333. We have addressed the reviewers' concerns in our response file. Additionally, the relevant information has been incorporated into the main text. We have also added a new section that addresses how linear classification performs in the presence of non-symmetric item space shapes. This study presents a mobile, single-point LDV system that offers rapid, in situ measurements of two-dimensional velocity vectors. A key advantage of this setup is its affordability and portability, making it ideal for laboratories without a full-scale LDV system. By manually navigating the probe in a predetermined pattern, users can collect enough data to calculate a two-dimensional velocity distribution. A programmable controller facilitates the synchronization of the probe's movement with the laser measurements, and the entire setup is manageable with a basic power supply and no sophisticated equipment. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this setup in retrieving two-dimensional flow information from three-dimensional data collected at various points in a flowing air stream around a wedge surface. This method offers an affordable, portable solution for individuals to conduct basic experiments and obtain 2D flow measurements in the absence of a full LDV system. Additionally, the presented setup can serve as a practical training tool for students to develop their experimental skills in the analysis of complex flows. It also has potential applications in fields such as aerospace, wind engineering, and environmental studies where two-dimensional flow measurements are often required but a full LDV system is not feasible due to cost or portability constraints. However, this method does come with certain limitations as evident from the obtained error margins in the experimental results. A comparison with corresponding theoretical values shows that the error margin for the flow regime considered in this study is around 5%. This method can potentially be improved further through the optimization of the probe's movement pattern and the incorporation of an acoustic signal follower to facilitate even distribution. This paper explores how to calculate the likelihood of a single event occurring within a set of reference events, all having the same underlying probability distribution. It constructs detailed frameworks for achieving this in both theoretical and practical contexts. Additionally, the paper discusses the challenges inherent in real-world data completeness and the methods employed to address these issues. Finally, the paper presents a concrete example illustrating the relevant concepts and tools. Although the concepts presented here are generally applicable, the specific discussion centers on the assessment of jet substructure phenomena studied in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. At the heart of this analysis lies a critical observation: when evaluating single events within many similar events, the total number of reference events is often unknown. Consequently, calculating the probability of the event in question becomes a complex problem lacking a straightforward solution. To overcome this hurdle, the paper develops two distinct methods - a theoretical approximation and a practical simulation - both facilitating accurate assessments. To address the associated computational hurdles, the paper presents a practical strategy for handling the issue of real-world data completeness. Lastly, the paper demonstrates the application of these concepts and tools through an actual event assessment, incorporating a realistic jet event as a case in point. The techniques outlined in this paper are likely to be of great use in a diverse range of fields, extending from high-energy physics to high-dimensional data analysis in machine learning. The number of points in a $d$-dimensional cube, $\mathbb{Z}^d$, that lie within a unit sphere, $S_{\infty}^{d-1}$, has been counted by many researchers. We take a different approach, focusing on finding the count of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that lie within a unit sphere, $S_{1}^{d-1}$, using the $L_1$-norm. Our method involves a polynomial-time algorithm that uses a binary search strategy and a recursive function to calculate the volume of a hyperplane section of the sphere. We also derive an asymptotic formula for the volume of the $L_1$-sphere, $V_{1}(d,r)$, and find a relation with a specific type of polynomial division problem, $P_{1,\alpha}(d,r)$. We further extend our approach to find the count of points in a $d$-dimensional cube that lie within a $k$-sided spherical prism, $S_{1}^{d-1,k}$. The results we obtain are useful for solving problems in different areas of mathematics, such as combinatorics, number theory, and algebraic topology. Moreover, these results have applications in the study of random walks and Brownian motion on graphs. We illustrate the generality of our approach by answering a question about the expected number of points in a $d$-dimensional cube that lie within a $k$-sided spherical prism, taking into account the uniform probability distribution of the starting point of a random walk in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. Neural speech synthesis models can learn natural speech patterns when given ample data, but they struggle to incorporate contextual information when generating speech, limiting their versatility. To address this, various contextual speech synthesis methods have been developed, often relying on supplementary frameworks or additional data, making them impractical for everyday use. This paper introduces MaskedSpeech, a novel approach that efficiently uses existing masks in speech representations to incorporate contextual information. This is done by treating masks as phonetic context markers and utilizing them to extract relevant character-level information from the input speech. When testing MaskedSpeech with the LJSpeech dataset, it showed significant improvements in speech quality and its effectiveness with minimal additional data. Additionally, it performed well in speech parody tasks, surpassing previous methods and demonstrating its capabilities in generating high-quality speech samples with specified characteristics. Code and model implementations are available for reproduction of the results at the specified URLs. One model implementation can generate speech samples with various acoustic properties simply by changing the input character-level information. This facilitates the production of speech samples in various languages and enables the synthesis of speech samples with specified characteristics, such as gender or accent. Additionally, it can be used to generate parasitic speech samples and perform speech parody tasks by providing a char-level mask as input. Notably, we find that non-parametric versions of this method have inherent problems, while parametric versions pose challenges due to the need for consistent estimation of the 'hidden space' map. However, under certain asymptotic conditions, we manage to establish the consistency of the predictive interval constructor. Our theoretical framework is grounded in non-parametric functional inference, where we also address related concerns such as checking if the 'hidden space' map is indeed informative. To overcome these challenges, a substantial knowledge gap must be bridged between the basic principle of neurocomputing and its practical implementation. A feasible approach to addressing this issue is to utilize proven concepts from neuroscience within software simulations, known as neural network emulators. Focusing on the Loihi brain-inspired chip, designed to learn from spatiotemporal patterns, this study developed an in-depth guide to facilitate bridging this gap. By closely modeling the Loihi chip's functionality within the Brian2 simulator, this work provides a comprehensive framework to simulate various neural network architectures similar to those employed on the actual chip. Moreover, a particular network architecture is showcased, which is an extension of a previous work, and is proven to be capable of learning and remembering temporal patterns through a process called temporal credit assignment. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of efficient hardware implementations, while also serving as a useful tool for investigating the underlying mechanisms of neuroinspired computing. This study reimagines the standard enhancement technique, commonly known as Digital Image Restoration, as a celebration of existing images, 'tinting' them with new and improved qualities.  By treating the enhancement process as a creative artistic endeavor, we harness the power of Generative Adversarial Networks to deliver an innovative, visually stunning method.  This novel approach boasts multiple advantages including increased artistic control, simplified training procedures, and the ability to differentiate between diverse and identical images.  To exemplify the efficacy of our method, we apply it to the color correction of celestial image scans.  The experiment's findings reveal that our celebration-based tinting technique surpasses the conventional enhancement method, maintaining the visual appeal of the original image while injecting improved and innovative qualities. The transformed celestial images are displayed in an online gallery, showcasing the artistic and innovative celebrations of the original images.  The CELEBRAPI technique is grounded in two complementary principles: Artistic Inspiration and Celebratory Training.  Artistic Inspiration encompasses the range of possible enhancements, 'tintings' that artistic agents might impose on original images.  Celebratory Training leverages a multi-objective assessment, celebrating the visual appeal of the original image while introducing innovative and exciting qualities through the 'tinting' process.  The direct utilization of artistic features might pose difficulties, as experts struggle to agree on the essential qualities.  To overcome this challenge, we devise an alternating training protocol for Generative Adversarial Networks, separating the celebration of image quality from the artistic tinting process.  The celebratory training is initially focused on achieving high image quality, with the artificial agents' objective function continuously updated as the training progresses to prioritize innovative and exciting 'tintings'.  The network is then reset, and the artistic tinting process is trained in parallel with the celebratory objective function, resulting in the celebration of interesting and visually appealing image qualities. Tb3RuO7 exhibits an unusual internal magnetic arrangement where Ru ions within a two-dimensional plane connected in a chain pattern possess a spin of 3/2 and are surrounded by Tb ions with a spin of 3/2 as well, creating an uneven magnetic field. This unique setup led to the occurrence of a partially disordered magnetic state called "trilinear magnetism" alongside the ordered "spin-polarized state" that emerged when the magnetic field's strength was increased. Trilinear magnetism is characterized by a unique internal magnetic arrangement where Ru and Tb ions are not uniformly aligned and this state persists until a critical temperature of 45 K. Upon reaching a critical magnetic field of 1.3 Tesla, the internal magnetic arrangement of Tb ions within the chain plane becomes evenly aligned in opposite directions, eliminating the disorder and resulting in a fully ordered "antiferromagnetic single-domain state". This process also caused the emergence of long-range ferromagnetic correlations that extended across the entire crystal. In contrast, long-range ferromagnetic correlations that formed in the spin-polarized state were confined to the internal magnetic arrangement of the Tb ions within the chain plane. Motivated by these findings, our research aims to investigate whether the proposed framework can effectively handle languages it wasn't initially trained on. Our results show that fine-tuning MidGPT on a small dataset yields superior performance gains in these languages, amounting to an average increase of 15.38 NLU metrics points and 12.60 FLU metrics points. Additionally, our data analysis reveals substantial room for improvement in NLP tasks for these languages, citing factors such as limited training data, language complexities, and the presence of non-Roman scripts, which present significant hurdles to overcome. To address these challenges, we suggest several strategic approaches to optimize BigScience multilingual frameworks for under-resourced languages, including the creation of more comprehensive training datasets, the development of language-specific adapters, and the design of task-sensitive fine-tuning objectives. Our findings, along with the accompanying code and language-specific data repositories, are now publicly accessible for evaluation purposes. Studying the development mass spectrum of dual binary systems via a dissipative simulation of a rotating matter stream that splits into two parts, researchers find that certain properties of the initial core determine the mass ratios of the resulting binaries. Specifically, if a core has minimal angular velocity, most systems develop equal masses, but when angular velocity increases, a greater proportion of binaries with equal masses transitions into those with significantly disparate masses. This trend indicates that more energetic systems produce fewer equal-mass binaries than those with lesser activity. Additionally, researchers find that no binary systems with equal masses originate from cores with extremely high angular velocity. Notably, if a core has rotational energy equivalent to a portion of the binding energy of the binary system, most developed binaries hold mass ratios near 0.5. Using statistical analysis, researchers conclude that active stellar systems would predominantly consist of binaries with roughly equal masses. This finding has implications for the development mass distributions found in multiple stellar systems and their potential connection to active galactic nuclei. Finally, researchers discuss how their findings can be applied to understanding the development mass distributions found in active galactic nuclei and other stellar systems. This work represents the initial step in examining the impact of core rotation on the development mass distributions of binary and multiple stellar systems. Future studies will focus on determining the global development mass distributions of binary systems and their correlation to the global angular momentum distributions of these cores. Furthermore, researchers aim to expand upon this framework by incorporating magnetic fields, which may supplement the production of unequal-mass binaries. By modeling active stellar systems as a rotating core that dissipates and fragments, researchers can identify key features of these cores that produce the observed distributions of binary mass ratios. This unique approach to understanding the development mass distributions of stellar systems is a key aspect of this work. Additionally, researchers discuss how their model can be used to explain the production of active galactic nuclei and their characteristic development mass distributions. The potential applications of this work extend to the study of multiple stellar systems and active galaxies, as well as the development mass distributions found in these phenomena. By analyzing the core properties of these objects, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of their internal dynamics and the production mechanisms of development mass distributions. This knowledge can also be applied to the study of active galaxies and multiple stellar systems, as these phenomena are thought to be fueled by similar core dynamics. By modeling these objects, researchers can identify key features of these cores that produce the observed development mass distributions. This work represents a crucial step in understanding the internal dynamics of these objects and their characteristic development mass distributions

To mitigate these concerns, the Cyberspace Administration of China launched an investigation into the severity of the problem. We employed the influence maximization problem solution from Facebook's study, utilizing features from the platforms involved to spread these rumors among specific individuals. Upon finding the optimal set of individuals to disseminate the digital rumors to, we analyzed the results under various assumptions and found that most users were unaware of the information being tracked by the government and that social media platforms were primary sources of digital rumors. Our assumed optimal spreaders showed a characteristic distribution among different age groups and that most digital rumors were spread through messaging apps like WeChat, revealing the need for the government to increase transparency about the information being tracked and to implement measures to prevent digital rumors through this surveillance. The accuracy of simulated NMR signals for a protein depends on the quality of its atomic model. Constructing detailed atomic models from quantum mechanics-based signals is a suitable approach for refining existing models. We demonstrate a method for placing atomic frameworks, starting from a set of NMR constraints and ending with a refined model, where all atoms are positioned within a predetermined uncertainty range. This involves an iterative process of framework installation, side chain arrangement, and non-bonded interaction adjustment until a satisfactory model is achieved. As a validation tool, the average displacement of amide proton N-H bonds serves as an accuracy metric for the entire protein. If the average displacement of these protons falls below a certain threshold (less than 0.3 Angstroms), the model is considered valid. We also provide criteria for the arrangement of protein side chains, including the relative angle of adjacent residues and the overall conformation of propanes, which, combined with the previously established protein framework, enable the generation of a reliable water model for future simulation studies. We examine how modifying the loss function affects a model's accuracy in classification tasks. Notably, our best approach, incorporating the Kullback-Leibler divergence with a weighted non-parametric estimator, demonstrates a 14% improvement in performance on domain adaptation tasks. A new approach based on a perturbation theory is presented for the calculation of many-body interactions within a method called parquet theory. This method revolves around the decomposition of a four-point vertex into lower-order interactions. Through a series of unitary transformations, the vertices of various orders are redefined in relation to a reference state, facilitating their calculation. Following a perturbation expansion, the Hamiltonian can be reformulated to incorporate these renormalized interactions, thereby yielding a perturbative correction to the original Hamiltonian. Notably, this correction is expressed through the summation of nested Feynman diagrams, which is the core concept of parquet theory. Furthermore, a diagrammatic representation is proposed that directly translates parquet theory's equations into the language of the Hamiltonian, thereby circumventing the need for a perturbative framework. This formulation maintains the self-consistency inherent to parquet theory. While derived primarily for the calculation of electron correlations, the parquet theory can also be applied to other areas of study, such as quantum field theories and condensed matter physics. However, its application may be hindered by the'sign problem' – a constraint specific to these fields – that prevents certain diagrammatic terms from being defined. These terms represent a significant component of the parquet theory's equations and, in the absence of a solution, may be omitted at the expense of accuracy, thereby reducing the scope of the theory. A related area of study, known as the vertex function approach, offers an alternative perspective that is immune to the constraints of the sign problem, thereby yielding complementary insights into the behavior of these systems. The present work seeks to reconcile these two formulations and, through a comparison of their respective strengths and weaknesses, provide a unified understanding of the relationship between the perturbative and diagrammatic views of parquet theory. The latter, in particular, holds the potential to develop new solutions to the sign problem that may shed light on the nature of this longstanding computational hurdle. The proposed formulation is expected to spawn a new area of research, which we term the 'Hamiltonian vertex approach'. The diagrammatic representation proposed herein is anticipated to facilitate the development of novel methods, such as those involving constrained path integrals, to tackle the sign problem. Finally, a range of research areas are identified that, although unrelated to the parquet theory, are expected to benefit from insights derived within the framework of this thesis, specifically in the domains of condensed matter physics, quantum field theories, and Higgs physics. Drawing on basic mechanisms from games and the study of dynamic learning systems, our analysis reveals that when instructors compete to achieve better student results, they will continuously strive for the optimal level of educational investment, causing student abilities to decline (or 'deteriorate) in the long term. However, if a limit is placed on how much educational resource expenditure is allowed, our model shows that heightened competition will actually lead to increased long-term investment in student abilities (or 'improvement). Our findings's significance is inspired by the 'Friedman Specification' of modern education, which is also reflected in other areas of society, such as the influence of merit-based education on social connections. Our study's major theme is the potential cost of achieving success through achievement. In addition, our research identifies common characteristics among areas of society where outcome-based success can be observed, including the connection between competitive dynamics and the tendency toward 'unfair' social hierarchies. Our model demonstrates that when instructors engage in a minimax game, where they collaborate to optimize a shared educational strategy, the resulting dynamic learning system not only achieves optimal student abilities but also invests the maximum amount in educational resources. To better understand the underlying principles of musical creation, we analyzed the structural organization of audio recordings from the past five decades, representing the most popular music of that time. Our analysis involved measuring the entropy of musical pieces by dividing them into 10-second segments and repeated this process for recordings from 1970 to 2020. We found that musical creation has become more predictable and consistent over the years, with variations in data complexity following a consistent pattern regardless of the specific time frame studied. Additionally, we identified a significant shift in music produced since the widespread adoption of digital technology in the 1990s, characterized by increased predictability. We compared our findings with the findings of a survey conducted among music enthusiasts, which showed similar patterns. Our study provides quantitative evidence of a link between musical creation and the technological advancements of the past century. The survey data also suggests a relationship between data complexity and individual creativity. We make an open-source software tool and a large dataset of musical creation available to the public to facilitate further research. Both can be accessed at: https://dc2020.github.io/ and https://github.com/DC2020/DCChallenge2020. We invite researchers from various fields to collaborate and help us understand the intricate nature of data complexity in musical creation. To successfully navigate complex environments in reward learning, agents need an effective evaluation system, pinpointing suboptimal policy versions. Currently, time-consuming human labeling is often necessary, but this paper offers a more efficient solution. By utilizing visual representations to augment ranking tasks, we've developed an approach that accurately connects conditional context features to preference scores. Our evaluation on a state-of-the-art DeepMind training platform reveals that human labels can be replaced with this method while maintaining training set quality. This replacement significantly reduces the financial costs associated with labeling, lowering estimated costs by a factor of 16. This economic benefit is achieved without adversely affecting the training outcome. Further experiments confirm the robustness of this approach, also yielding reliable results on a public dataset in the field of medical concept evaluation. Overall, this method's success relies on two key components: first, cluster models that efficiently capture environment characteristics, and second, a proprietary algorithm facilitating efficient query optimization. As a result, this solution offers an attractive middle ground between fully automated systems and the existing reliance on extensive human labeling. Its development and utilization could accelerate the advancement of reward learning and related fields, encompassing topics like medical concept evaluation and document classification. A standardized method of analyzing extreme value events utilizes a reduced data set that represents the occurrence of rare events via a Poisson process over gradually increasing thresholds. Traditional parameterizations, focusing on quantiles or quantile-based measures like quantile estimates, present difficulties in simulating examples and estimating parameters, particularly for more complex distributions like the generalized extreme value distribution. This paper proposes a novel approach to estimating parameters for a specific type of extreme value distribution, the power law outward (PLO) distribution, utilizing a simplified method of modeling the standardized data set. We compare the proposed approach with established techniques that use quantile parameterizations and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations and a case study involving extreme temperature data. A relevant extension of the proposed method to other extreme value distributions is also provided. The proposed method, known as PAR4EL, is an alternative to existing extreme value estimation methods that addresses difficulties associated with quantile parameterizations, and its extensions will be implemented in the R package PAR4EL.

In the field of Offline Reinforcement Learning, we approach the issue of handling corrupted datasets in RL. Differing from traditional learning damage, dataset corruption in RL leads to flawed policy decisions and compromised safety. Present methods for evaluating dataset reliability rely on the quality of a well-trained, offline policy, however, we demonstrate that such methods are susceptible to failure when faced with optimally-designed corrupted datasets.

Instead, we develop a new framework to assess the impact of corrupted data on RL training. We further propose a method for enhancing the robustness of offline RL training, involving the optimization of a robust policy that excels across various levels of dataset corruption. Through experimentation using simulated and real-world scenarios, such as a mobile robot navigating a 2D world, we successfully apply our approach and show significant improvements over existing methods on a publicly available benchmark. Notably, we achieve comparable performance to the baseline method, called GO-PF, while ensuring the trained policy remains 30% more resilient to corruption. We also evaluate the limitations of our approach and the challenges that come with handling corrupted data in RL. Our work aims to promote the development of more robust RL methods, focusing on corruption-resistance, and enabling safer decision-making in real-world scenarios.

The capacity of a language model to handle text not seen during training is crucial, and we developed an approach to supply a language model with information about its own performance outside of its training data. We present a framework of text categories based on semantic relationships and find that many out-of-distribution texts fall into two main categories. To further refine this system and improve models' performance on out-of-distribution data, we provide labeled datasets of texts that are out-of-distribution for specific models. Using this framework and these datasets, we show that a language model's level of out-of-distribution performance can be predicted before actual testing and that models that do well out-of-distribution are less likely to fall into the more challenging category of text. Additionally, we find that using adaptation techniques along with our identified categories allows a model to better handle out-of-distribution data and improves its performance. Our work and data are now available online. We anticipate that identifying the categories of out-of-distribution texts and using adaptation techniques within those categories could lead to better-predicted and potentially distributed applications of language models. We propose that a model should first be trained on its core dataset and then undergo training within the specific out-of-distribution data categories that it is likely to encounter. This could lead to enhanced and adaptable language models that are capable of effectively handling a range of texts beyond their training data. Traditionally, molecular engines are imagined as having a rotational dynamics similar to that of a Brownian motor. However, the unique physics of tunneling currents, which involve electron and molecule attachment and detachment, suggests a more erratic and unpredictable movement. Inspired by this physics, a more realistic model of molecular engines is developed, one that incorporates sudden changes in the molecule's state and the action of tunneling rates that fluctuate in response to the molecule's position. Utilizing this "jump" model, even the simplest molecular engines, powered by a single tunneling path, can still operate efficiently as motors. Additionally, this model provides a possible explanation for recent experiments observing non-Boltzmann behavior of scattered electrons and indicates that, under certain conditions, an equilibrium tunneling current can generate thermal motion in a molecule, even when in equilibrium. It is anticipated that this model will be a crucial framework for the design and optimization of molecular engines. Furthermore, this model also addresses the feasibility of generating a wide range of power outputs in molecular engines, highlighting their potential to enhance the performance of future electronic and mechanical devices. Finally, this model also raises the question of whether it is possible to cool a molecular engine below its natural temperature, which could be an important area of study in the field of molecular engineering. It is anticipated that this research will be a significant contribution to the field: the study of molecular engineering driven by tunneling currents. Finally, this research also raises the question of whether it is possible to extend this model to other types of molecular engines, such as those powered by light. Several studies have established that, given two finite automata, it is possible to determine whether they can mimic each other's behavior within a specified language, and the associated decision problem lies in the class coNP. In contrast, the issue of whether an arbitrary finite automaton can replicate another one's transitions is a coNP-complete problem. We now investigate a related concept called unidirectional resynchronizability in finite automata, which involves determining if two finite automata can be modified to recognize the same language by aligning their transitions in a single direction. Notably, we find that deciding unidirectional resynchronizability is only possible in polynomial time for finite automata with a restricted structure. However, the problem becomes more complex (coNP-complete) when dealing with general finite automata. Nonetheless, the associated decision problem remains a more tractable member of the class of NP-complete problems. We also explore some additional properties of term transducers, including a specific type of unidirectional resynchronizability, for which the associated decision problem lies in the class NP. Lastly, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to determine whether a finite automaton can mimic the behavior of another one, provided that both automata recognize the same language. The underlying idea employs a novel technique to establish a connection between finite automata and a specific type of graph. The result is a more efficient solution to a problem that was previously addressed in the literature using different approaches. Additionally, the paper provides an efficient algorithm for determining whether two finite automata can be modified to recognize the same language by aligning their transitions in a single direction. The study also extends some of the proposed decision problems to their optimization counterparts. Notably, we prove that solving these optimization problems is either possible in polynomial time or requires a time that is proportional to the square of the input size. The underlying idea involves providing a suitable approximation scheme for the underlying problem. The decision problems that we investigate pertain to the behavior of two finite automata, for which we seek to determine if they can be modified to recognize the same language by aligning their transitions in a single direction. In recent years, generalized convolutions have been utilized in a variety of fields. We propose an efficient method to compute generalized convolutions more quickly than the traditional brute force approach, which involves generating all possible combinations of lengths. We examine two specific types of generalized convolutions, known as $D$-convolution and $N$-convolution, which can be calculated using our found asymptotic upper limits for their computation. These upper limits are based on established algorithms for the longest common subsequence problem. Additionally, we provide a more streamlined approach for $N$-convolution that eliminates the need for extra memory, making it suitable for memory-constrained systems. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method through a comparative study, conducted using a wide range of lengths, objects, and algorithms. The results demonstrate that our approach is both faster and more efficient than the brute force method. Regarding memory usage, our method shows substantial improvements, with a key finding that our $N$-convolution approach can run 8-27 times longer without running out of memory compared to the brute force method. Furthermore, our method is specifically optimized for calculating object counts and can perform this task at a fraction of the energy required by the brute force approach. We provide a thorough explanation of our method, known as the BPS algorithm, which is designed to conserve energy and memory, even when running multiple calculations concurrently. The BPS algorithm is a significant innovation that is expected to be a valuable tool in statistical physics research. The associated data and source codes for this study are publicly available at https://github.com/charlierippe/generalized_convolution. Additionally, the underlying physical model that inspired our approach is described in an accompanying paper, also available on the arXiv server (arXiv:2202.05299). The dynamic mode decomposition technique has gained recognition for its ability to analyze complex data by automatically identifying significant patterns, but it has a significant drawback - it can easily be misled by noise. Despite this limitation, the technique remains popular, with researchers continuously developing new variants to improve its robustness. One such approach is the linear and nonlinear clarification optimization method, which uses a kernel function to create a more stable representation of the dynamic mode decomposition, with results showing a notable improvement over the original dynamic mode decomposition and other variants such as the sparse identification of dynamics and the residual component analysis, particularly in a simulation study using synthetic data and a real-world aircraft ride case. When applied to the aircraft ride case, the approach identified coherent structures consistent with physical expectations and demonstrated the ability to clarify ambiguous patterns, with results indicating a significant enhancement of the dynamic mode decomposition, with the advantage of being a post-processing technique that can be applied to existing results. With this modification, the dynamic mode decomposition technique can now provide more reliable insights from noisy data, with the potential to significantly expand its applications in modern dynamic analysis. This paper introduces a groundbreaking research approach to examine the impact of push forces on the landing phase of vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) aircraft, particularly those with traditional pusher propulsion. A pusher configuration can affect the vehicle's landing dynamics due to the displacement of rotor downwash from the landing area, potentially leading to a softer landing and increased pusher thrust requirements. To investigate the influence of pusher thrust, we utilize an open-source nonlinear analytical model, which accurately represents the landing phase dynamics of a pusher-configured VTOL aircraft. A key model assumption is that the rotor downwash can be accurately predicted using a porous disk model, thereby enabling the separation of the vehicle's dynamics into independent subsystems. We confirm the validity of the model through comparisons with numerical and experimental integration methods, and conduct sensitivity analyses on the vehicle's state variables and pusher thrust signals. A key outcome is that the model's ability to separate the vehicle's dynamics into distinct subsystems facilitates the identification of optimal pusher thrust signals that reduce landing impacts and enhance vehicle stability. Furthermore, we observe that the pusher thrust signals are influenced by the vehicle's state variables, particularly due to the interaction of the rotor downwash with the landing struts, and highlight the potential for pusher thrust to counteract negative aerodynamic forces and improve landing stability. Lastly, we note that the model's analytical structure, enabled by the separation of the vehicle's dynamics and the utilization of the porous disk model, significantly reduces the computational requirements for solving the nonlinear equations, thereby enabling the rapid evaluation of various flight scenarios and enabling learning for VTOL aircraft design. We anticipate that this open-source model will contribute to the development of more efficient pusher-propelled VTOL aircraft, and provide a useful tool for designing vehicles that can operate safely and efficiently within their performance limits. Additionally, we believe that the model's analytical structure will facilitate the adoption of machine learning and other optimization techniques to push the limits of vehicle performance, while also ensuring safe operation. We intend to explore these opportunities in future research.

To facilitate more efficient visual navigation, we propose MemoNav, an agent that memorizes key observations during its training period and then utilizes these reminders to achieve better navigation results. MemoNav's memory is organized in two distinct components: 1) a map database storing spatially-indexed scenes, and 2) a time-oriented event log recording the agent's historical experiences. When navigating, MemoNav activates a self-recall mechanism to selectively retrieve insightful remembrances from the agent's past experiences and incorporates them into a reward-shaping system to guide the agent's decision-making. Through this innovative design, MemoNav demonstrates improved navigation capabilities, particularly on complex navigation tasks, and also showcases better generalizability on various navigation scenarios. Our experimental findings indicate that MemoNav's reliance on past experiences enhances its navigation performance, and the agent's memory management is instrumental in selecting relevant reminders to shape the agent's behavior. A theoretical framework has been developed to model spin-orbit coupled systems with attractive interactions, using a hard core boson description. Within this framework, a general approach is taken to derive spin-orbit coupled versions of the Hugenholtz-Nagami condition and the momentum distribution theorem. By applying this framework to a two-band Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions, a particular limit of the model is analyzed, in which the spin-orbit coupling parameter $\kappa$ is much smaller than the on-site interaction $\lambda$. Within this regime, a linear regression analysis is used to investigate the spin-orbit coupling's impact on pair condensate momentum, in the presence of single particle momentum condensate. Our findings reveal that under certain conditions, a superfluid momentum condensate forms, characterized by an effective topological superfluidity $\kappa$ and a related topological spin susceptibility. Through numerical simulations, a notable spin susceptibility peak is observed when the Rashba interaction's strength is equivalent to the on-site interaction's strength. The topological superfluidity $\kappa$ and spin susceptibility $K$ exhibit Type-I regime transitions, in which we have identified first and second order phase transition boundaries. Furthermore, under specific conditions, a spin singlet topological superfluid phase is predicted, in which both spin-orbit coupled and non-spin-orbit coupled systems exhibit a similar topological superfluidity $\kappa$. Our theoretical predictions are both spin-orbit coupled and non-spin-orbit coupled, in agreement with recent experimental observations. The proposed topological superfluidity $d=\kappa+\lambda$ can now be generated solely by the spin-orbit coupling parameter $\kappa$. The spin susceptibility $K$ exhibits analogies with the weakly coupled superconducting state, in which it is proportional to $\lambda/\kappa$ or $\lambda/\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the gap parameter. The predicted spin susceptibility $K$ is also robust against changes in the Rashba interaction's strength. The proposed spin-orbit coupled bosonic framework provides a general approach to model spin-orbit coupled systems with attractive interactions, in which a spin susceptibility $K$ and topological superfluidity $\kappa$ are simultaneously present. The predicted spin-orbit coupled bosonic phase diagram is both topologically non-trivial and diverse, consisting of a spin-orbit coupled superfluid, spin-orbit coupled Mott insulator, and spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensate phases. Specifically, it requires at least k local measurements to determine the position of every vertex in the graph. The minimum number of such local measurements needed for a soluble graph is known as the graph's metric dimension, denoted by McD(G). In contrast, the simplified metric dimension, denoted by N McD ( G ), represents the minimum number of vertices required to locate the graph, where these vertices may use the graph's original metric. Here, the concept of simplified metric dimension is explored, with a corresponding metric space formulation that helps determine the simplified metric dimension's lower and upper bounds for specific graph types. Furthermore, the study establishes a relationship between the simplified metric dimension and the graph's minimum degree. Additionally, several open issues and potential directions for further research are proposed. The work also provides a parameterized algorithm for calculating the simplified metric dimension. Notably, while the approach is designed to work efficiently when the number of vertices is relatively small, it may not be suitable for large-scale graphs due to its high computational complexity. This research develops an innovative technology to efficiently remove sulfur dioxide from flue gas using a combination of ozone and ultraviolet radiation. A specific UV lamp is identified that can activate ozone within a reactor with a minimal size of 0.01 m^3 per unit. A unique ozone-UV scheme is developed that not only fits within a standard 40-foot shipping container but also filters the flue gas through an electrostatic precipitator to remove large particulate matter before being treated. The treatment process itself has two stages: the first stage uses ozone and UV radiation to achieve nearly complete SOx removal with a high efficacy of 99.9% and a energy consumption of 0.25 kWh/Nm^3; the second stage uses only ozone to remove any remaining SOx with a further removal efficiency of 38.5% and an energy consumption of 0.16 kWh/Nm^3. The overall removal efficiency of sulfur dioxide is over 99% with a high energy consumption of 0.42 kWh/Nm^3. This technology is particularly suitable for small-scale power plants and heating systems in China. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, designers face a challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Current simulation tools have limitations, such as being architecture-specific, user-friendly, and capable of concurrent execution. To address these issues, we have developed a new simulation framework that offers a number of features, including a portable and simplified model of neuromorphic cores, a hybrid phase execution mode, and extended transaction types. This framework is based on SystemC and provides an easy-to-use API for designing and simulating neuromorphic computing systems. To evaluate its effectiveness, we have used the framework to model and simulate a network of learning-based neural processors, demonstrating its ability to accurately simulate complex systems. Experimental results show that the framework is capable of concurrent execution, with a simulation speed-up of up to 2.4 times compared to a pure transaction-based simulation approach. Furthermore, we have verified the framework's accuracy and evaluated its performance using a standard benchmark, as well as exploring its potential for distributed computing and energy-aware design optimization. Overall, this framework offers a versatile tool for designing and simulating neuromorphic computing systems. This paper introduces a novel machine learning approach called Indecision Forests, a random forest equivalent that incorporates argument-based reasoning while handling uncertainty. It employs quantified ambiguity as its decision rule and demonstrates fissionability in relation to the polynomial hierarchy. Our model can be utilized for both supervised classification and regression tasks. Additionally, we propose a training method and an evaluation framework that incorporates the computability of its tree structures. Our empirical study, conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets, reveals that Indecision Forests can achieve up to a 20% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art machine learning models. Furthermore, we provide evidence that cross-validation is effective only when the dataset is finitely decid able. This research has implications in AI, highlighting the importance of carefully selecting test datasets to evaluate models equitably. In recent years, DTW has experienced increased attention, particularly among experts in pattern recognition and time series, due to its effective alignment capabilities. However, DTW's high computational complexity has significant implications, including a lengthy pre-processing time and high memory requirements for comparing large time series data. To address these challenges, this study proposes an optimized DTW variation, known as PrunedDTW, to reduce complexity and accelerate the discarding process. Building on PrunedDTW, we develop a modified version, Early Discarding PrunedDTW (ED PrunedDTW), to enhance discard decisions and improve alignment computation. We then apply PrunedDTW and ED PrunedDTW to time series classification and similarity search tasks, yielding superior outcomes and faster processing speeds compared to the original PrunedDTW. Notably, our research indicates that PrunedDTW and ED PrunedDTW can be seamlessly integrated into existing DTW-based systems as an enhancement. Furthermore, we introduce a novel strategy for early discard decisions, which expands the PrunedDTW's discard criterion, resulting in enhanced decisions and faster alignment computation. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments using the MSRC-16 dataset under different error margins and compared the performance of PrunedDTW and ED PrunedDTW against two state-of-the-art algorithms: DTW and OptimalDTW. The results reveal that PrunedDTW and ED PrunedDTW achieve significant gains in processing time and early discard decisions, while also outperforming DTW and OptimalDTW in similarity search accuracy and classification rates. Moreover, we present the theoretical justification for early discard decisions, which enables the determination of optimal thresholds and optimal alignment computation. Based on these findings, we present an influential variation, ED PrunedDTW$^{opt}$, which yields the best possible performance among all variants. Finally, we apply PrunedDTW and its improvements to real-world datasets, demonstrating the efficacy of early discard decisions in simultaneously reducing processing time and boosting classification rates or similarity search accuracy. The proposed PrunedDTW and its variants provide a significant contribution to the time series community by opening new avenues for research and development. The proposed PrunedDTW and its variations can be seamlessly integrated into existing DTW-based systems as an enhancement and offer a new strategy to achieve similar or better results while reducing processing time. The PrunedDTW and its variations can also be applied to other areas beyond time series classification and similarity search, including similarity search in second-order data and image classification. However, this has created a gap between the theoretical concepts of software testing and their practical application, causing students to feel overwhelmed with the subject's novelty. To bridge this gap, innovative educational tools incorporate game-like elements and instant feedback into the learning process of software testing. Building on these advancements, this study presents a novel, inquiry-based approach to conceptual remarks (NBCR) that integrates instant feedback into the learning process. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of NBCR to revitalize the conventional method, paving the way for further research into the development of more sophisticated educational tools. In many domains, explanations are necessary to guarantee the quality of models. However, the explanations offered by DNNs are often difficult to verify due to their interpretive nature. This study addresses this issue by introducing a system that explains DNN predictions through ILP (Inference Logic Programming) based rule sets. The rules capture key 'concept' traits, enabling them to describe regions within the input space and associated outputs. The system uses an efficient, analytic approach to create these rule sets. Since ILP based explanations are verifiable and easy to use in various contexts, the study merges this method with concept analysis to provide a deeper understanding of DNN behavior. The resulting system, called CEMD, offers explanations in a logical, easy to reason about format, thus addressing the current limitations of DNN explanations. This approach is distinct from other explanation techniques and is not confused with the underlying DNN model. This system has been tested on three different datasets and the results show that ILP based explanations are preferred over DNN based explanations. Additionally, the study found that combining CEMD with DNN explanations provided a more comprehensive understanding of DNN behavior. The study's findings are two-fold: Firstly, ILP based explanations outperform DNN based explanations; Secondly, the combination of CEMD with DNN explanations offers a more comprehensive understanding of DNN behavior. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been successful in learning node representations for graph-based data. However, their convolutional components, which combine the features of connected nodes, can also amplify errors. This study investigates the sensitivity of GCN's convolutional part to noise in labeled nodes, demonstrating that the network is highly susceptible to perturbations in its features. Through this analysis, we identify the parameters that influence the network's vulnerability to noise and propose a range of methods to improve its robustness. Experiment results on multiple graph classification and node classification benchmarks reveal that our simple yet effective approaches surpass current state-of-the-art robustness techniques by substantial margins. Internet Service Providers have long faced challenges in managing network bandwidth,
leading to poor internet experience for users. To resolve this, ISPs have negotiated
payment agreements with content providers, with the aim of improving network
quality and generating additional revenue. However, these payments have become a
significant expense for content companies, which are now seeking alternatives to
recoup their costs. Given the prominence of profit sharing agreements between
content and service providers, our research delves into the legal and technical
aspects of these agreements, while proposing a novel model that enables content
providers to influence the quality of service and increase it in proportion to the
reciprocal payments received from ISPs. Through numerical examples, the benefits of
this model can be demonstrated. Additionally, the analysis is grounded in existing
laws, with a particular focus on the ongoing debate surrounding zero-rating
policies. By examining the relationship between payments and service quality, our
research provides insight into the trade-offs involved in profit distribution agreements.

These factors, induced by the beating motion of the heart and varying tissue types, cause additive and shifting distortions in the signal. The proposed approach addresses these interference factors by modeling them as convolutional transforms and incorporating this information into feature extraction. The research showcases the effectiveness of considering the convolutive distortion in signal processing, an aspect previously overlooked in prior studies. In this framework, a nation's climate action is driven by a partnership index, representing the level of international cooperation. A system of first-order differential equations is employed to model the dynamics of this index. Solutions to the equations indicate that in the absence of climate action costs, all nations will work together to address climate change. However, when such costs are introduced, the model exhibits a Hopf bifurcation, leading to oscillating patterns of cooperation. This modification leads to the degradation of climate cooperation. A numerical study reveals that increased variability in the rates at which nations adopt climate policies hastens this degradation. This study investigates the concept of trustworthiness in a second-price auction setting, comprising two stages.  Bidders compete in an auction for a single item, and the auction winner is selected through a random drawing.  The bidder submitting the highest bid in the first stage pays the second-highest bid amount.  We discovered that bids exhibited a mix of strategic and non-strategic elements.  Strategic bidding dominated in the initial bids, but the second bids often fell short of optimal levels, suggesting a non-strategic component exists.  We also found that bidders who exhibited strategic thinking in the first stage tended to be less strategic in the second stage.  Notably, a subset of bidders demonstrated a willingness to sacrifice monetary gains to ensure other bidders submitted higher bids, defining trustworthiness in this context.  We further discovered that the majority of bidders prefer a trustworthiness-level-based pricing scheme (paying the second-highest bid) over a fairness-level-based scheme (paying the average of all bids).  Finally, we observed that bidders' bids were more strategic, and trustworthiness was displayed to a greater degree when the auction winner's payment is based on the second-highest bid rather than the average of all bids.  These results have been translated into policy recommendations for digital auction environments.  We suggest that platform owners facilitate a trustworthy environment by clearly communicating the auction mechanism, potentially through a voluntary contribution mechanism that makes bidding strategies more sustainable.  We also propose that increased transparency and trustworthiness in digital auctions could lead to a reduction in the use of automated bidding tools.  Furthermore, the adoption of a voluntary contribution mechanism might assist in promoting a more efficient and sustainable bidding strategy.  Finally, we observed that the willingness to sacrifice monetary gains for the sake of trustworthiness could be utilized as an implicit preference, enabling the design of auctions that better align with bidders' overall preferences. We explore the regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, examining their structure through two main approaches. Firstly, geometric vertex partitions provide insight into the Coxeter orbit space, with individual orbits corresponding to distinct partitions. Secondly, combining ideals related to Hessenberg subspaces with specific d-vector sequences yields a vast family of Gr\"obner monomial ideals, whose Gr\"obner fans mirror the Coxeter orbit space. As the Hessianber variety degenerates, its maximal torus weights span a significant, finite subset of the positive lattice, corresponding to Frobenius separations within the Gr\"obner fan. This leads to the construction of a comprehensive, finite set of Gr\"obner basis generators for the Hessianber variety, via its associated ideals in type A. Furthermore, using geometric vertex partitions, and exploiting symmetry, enables a comprehensive description of the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety of type B. Additionally, the key concept of 'Frobenius crystals' emerges, with a notable example being the regular semisimple Hessenberg variety, whose Gr\"obner structure can also be fully realized. Moreover, the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety of type C exhibits a degeneration, whose Coxeter orbit space corresponds to a set of accessible, finite-ranked posets. In a broader context, this variety represents a significant instance of a 'Frobenius model' for a homogeneous space, with potential connections to the study of Lie superalgebras and a generalization of the 'Frobenius method' to classical invariant theory. Finally, the techniques employed in this research are also applicable to a broader range of 'Hessenberg varieties of type C', with a generalization to the 'Hessenberg varieties of type D'. With a few exceptions, this study achieves a comprehensive characterization of the regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of any Lie type. To facilitate future study, we provide a comprehensive, accessible introduction to the 'Frobenius method' and its recent developments, also outlining the likely future research path. We also provide the Gr\"obner basis generators for the Hessenberg variety in type A. The code used for the degeneration and Gr\"obner basis computation is available at https://github.com/martinoconnor/FrobeniusModels. This research was previously presented at the 2022 Seattle Joint Conference in Algebra and Topology. The associated journal talk is at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.004

In our study, we investigate the characteristics of neutrino-type instability in three-dimensional simulations of core-collapse supernovae. This type of instability occurs when a neutrino group becomes disconnected from the others, leading to a neutrino group's density decreasing inside an equilibrium distribution. We observe this phenomenon in multiple simulations, typically after the shock wave has reversed direction and is re-establishing itself. This neutrino instability is found to be most pronounced in simulations where the core is still undergoing contraction and when the instability affects ions. When it occurs in a region where electrons and nuclei have reached equilibrium, the instability has minimal impact on the fluid's velocity. Notably, this type of instability is found to be common in simulations, albeit its influence on the supernova's overall structure is found to be relatively small. This suggests that while it may contribute to other aspects of the supernova, it is unlikely to affect its overall development. This work is part of a series exploring common phenomena found in supernova simulations, focusing on their characteristics and features. This research does not draw any conclusions about the potential effects of these phenomena but instead aims to provide a detailed overview of the phenomena themselves.
